t.17.2: He who, content and with pure senses, ever delights in solitude has attained the fruit of knowledge and likewise the fruit of the practice of yoga.
t.17.3: Ah, the knower of truth is never distressed in this world, for this whole sphere of the universe is filled by that One alone.
t.17.4: These sense-objects, whatever they may be, never delight one who rejoices in the Self, just as nimba leaves do not delight an elephant that relishes sallakī leaves.
t.17.6: Here in saṃsāra one sees the man who longs for enjoyment, and also the man who longs for liberation; but rare indeed is the great-souled one who craves neither enjoyment nor liberation.
t.17.5: But one who is not tainted by pleasures once they have been enjoyed, and who has no longing for those not yet enjoyed, such a person is rare in this world.
t.17.7: For one whose mind is truly noble, there is indeed nothing to be rejected or accepted in dharma, wealth, pleasure, or liberation, nor likewise in life or in death.
t.17.8: He has no longing for the dissolution of the universe, nor any aversion to its continuance. Therefore the blessed one lives happily on whatever livelihood comes to him.
t.17.9: Thinking, 'By this knowledge I have attained my goal,' the accomplished one, whose mind has dissolved, abides at ease, seeing, hearing, touching, smelling and eating.
t.17.11: He neither wakes nor sleeps, he neither opens his eyes nor closes them. Ah, the supreme state of one whose mind is liberated prevails everywhere!
t.17.10: In one for whom the ocean of saṃsāra has dried up, the gaze is empty, action is purposeless, and the senses are inactive; there is neither longing nor detachment.
t.17.12: Everywhere he is seen to be at ease in himself, everywhere pure of heart; freed from all latent impressions, the liberated one shines everywhere.
t.17.13: Seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, taking, speaking and walking, the great-souled one, freed from striving and non-striving, is truly liberated.
t.17.14: The liberated one neither blames nor praises, neither rejoices nor grows angry, neither gives nor takes; he is free of attachment to anything everywhere.
t.17.15: Seeing a woman full of passion, or death drawing near, the great-souled one remains unshaken in mind and abides in himself; he is truly liberated.
t.17.16: For the steadfast one who sees with an equal eye everywhere, there is no distinction at all between pleasure and pain, man and woman, prosperity and adversity.
t.17.17: In the man whose wandering in saṃsāra has come to an end, there is no violence, nor indeed compassion, no arrogance and no humility, no wonder, nor indeed any agitation.
t.17.18: The liberated one neither hates the objects of the senses nor craves them; with a mind ever unattached, he experiences whatever is attained and whatever is not attained.
t.17.19: He whose mind is empty does not know the distinctions of concentration and non-concentration, of good and harm; he remains as if established in aloneness.
t.17.20: Free from the sense of 'mine,' free from ego, firmly convinced that nothing is, with all desires melted away within, he does not act even while acting.
t.17.21: Free from the mind's shining forth, from delusion, dream and dullness, the one whose mind has melted away would have reached some indescribable state.
